full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha CJ: Two questions are involved in these appeals and petitions. The first question is whether if a company incorporated under the Companies Act commits an offence punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is excluded from prosecution, can a director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company be prosecuted for that offence, and secondly, whether if more than one cheques issued by the same drawer can be prosecuted in a single case. 

 2. The respondents instituted complaints against the petitioners. In the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka for allegedly committing offence under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, alleging, inter alia, that the petitioners purchased some raw materials for consumption of their factory, Madaripur Spinning Mills Ltd. The petitioners paid the price of cotton by 22 (twenty two) different cheques to the complainants. All the cheques were dishonoured on different dates due to insufficiency of fund and also as per instruction of the petitioner No.1 for not honouring them. Consequent upon which, the complainants issued legal notices requesting the petitioners to make payments with-in 30 days of the dates of receipt of the notices. The petitioners despite receipt of the notices did not make payment within the statutory period and accordingly, the complaints were made for prosecution of the petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Thereafter, learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate on examination of the complainants issued processes under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against the petitioners, and after compliance of formalities, transmitted the case records to the Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka for trial. The cases were taken up for trial by the learned Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, before whom, the' petitioners filed applications under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure for their discharge on the plea that charges are groundless. The learned Metropolitan Additional Sessions judge heard the parties at length and by orders dated 2nd July, 2009, and 15th October, 2009, respectively discharged the accused petitioners on the reasoning that as the Madaripur Spinning Mills Ltd. or its Managing Director or other officers or office bearers have not been made accused in the complaint petitions, the cases are not legally maintainable. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid orders the complainants moved the High Court Division for quashing the proceedings. In respect of Criminal Petition Nos. 533 and 534 of 2010, Dynamic Textile Industries Limited issued the cheques in favour of Complainant named Binoy Krishna Sikdar, who was also one of the complainants in the complaint that brought Criminal Appeals No. 7-22. The cheques were dishonored on similar ground. 

 3. The High Court Division observed that the companies are also liable to be prosecuted and punished along with its Directors and other officers who acted on behalf of the companies; that in the absence of the companies there is no legal bar to proceed with the cases against the Directors or officers of the companies who were responsible for carrying out the activities on behalf of the companies; that there is no mandatory prohibition that in the absence of the companies as accused, the prosecution against other accused persons who acted on behalf of the companies would fail and that in the absence of such legal bar, the criminal proceedings initiated against the Directors and Managers of the companies would be maintainable. 

 4. The moot question is whether the proceedings are legally maintainable in the absence of the Companies which committed the offence punishable under action 138. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants argued that the High Court Division failed to consider that since the cheques in question were issued by the company, it is the company which has committed the offence under section 140 read with section 138 and therefore, the proceedings cannot be legally maintainable in the absence of the company being arraigned as an accused in the case, inasmuch as, there is mandatory provision of law to make the company as accused in the case. His second contention is that when a cheque drawn by a company is returned for any cause, the person responsible in the affairs of the company as well as the company shall be responsible within the meaning of section 140. The expressions used in sub-section (2) of section 140 "with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary-or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty for that offence" clearly indicate that if the offence is committed by a company, the company being the principal offender no proceeding can legally be maintainable against such Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer of the company. In the absence of the company, and such Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer only be liable to be prosecuted if it can be shown that the offence has been committed with their consent or connivance. 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where any offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent for connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly: 

 8. A combined reading of sub-sections (l) and (2) of section 140 would discern three categories of persons to be brought within the ambit of section 138, through legal fiction envisaged therein the first category is the Company which committed the offence; the second category is every person who was in-charge of and was responsible for the business of the company at the time of commission of offence; and the third category is, any other person who' is a Director, Manager, Secretary of officer of the company, with whose connivance or neglect, the company has committed the offence. Though sub-section (1) of section 138 speaks of a drawer of the cheque who would alone have been the offender of the offence, because of section 140, penal liability has been cast on other persons connected with the company. The difference between sections 138 and 140 is that in respect of section 138 the offence is committed by human being that is to say, natural person and in section 140 though the expression "the person" is used which is qualified by a company which means "any body corporate and includes a firm of other association of individuals" which is a juristic person or not. It can be prosecuted for the offence under section 138. 

 13. Next question is about the service of notice. Despite the dishonour of the cheque, if no notice is served upon the drawer of the cheque within the stipulated time fixed by the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 138 regarding the return of the cheque and if the drawer of the cheque fails to make payment of the amount of money covered by the cheque within thirty days of receipt of the notice, no cause of action for such commission of offence will arise within the meaning of section 141(b). If a notice is issued upon the Managing Director of the company who is in-charge of the affairs of the Company and signed the cheque on behalf of the company, the service of notice upon the Managing Director is sufficient to infer that the company has received the notice. This will fasten the company as well as the commission of the offence. This is because the Managing Director being the chief executive of-the company his knowledge may be deemed to be the knowledge of the company. 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where' an offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any, neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company such director manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. 

 15. A complaint was filed against, the Managing Director and the Production! Manager of the said Company for violation of the offences mentioned above. The accused persons moved a petition for quashing the proceedings against them on the ground that they could not, in law, be prosecuted unless the company itself was prosecuted. Their contention was overruled by the 

 16. In a latter case in UP Pollution Control Board vs Ms Modi Distillery, AIR 1988 SC 1128, similar question arose. In that case, a complaint was launched against M/s. Modi Distillery, its Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Managing Director and members of the Board of Directors of M/s. Modi Industries Ltd, the company owning the industrial unit for commission of offence under section 44 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 which is punishable under section 47 of the said Act. Section 47 of the said Act is analogous to section 17 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (India). This section 47 of Act 1974, is worded in the same language of section 10 of Act, 1955. The High Court quashed the proceedings on the ground that there could not be vicarious liability saddled on the Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Managing Director and other members of the Board of Directors of the Company under section 47 of the Act unless there was prosecution of the company, Mis Modi Industries Ltd. The question arose in the Supreme Court was whether the Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Managing Director and members of the Board are liable to be proceeded against in the absence of the prosecution of the company. The Supreme Court on construction of section 47 of Act, 1974 was of the view that the Chairman, Vice- Chairman, Managing Director and the members of the Board could be prosecuted as having been in-charge of and responsible to the company for the business of the industrial unit Mis Modi Distillery owned by it and could be deemed to be guilty of the offence with which they are charged. It was also held that even if there was any technical flow it was a curable flow that could be removed by having remitted the matter to the Chief Judicial Magistrate with a direction to the company as the accused. The Court, however, observed: 

 25. Two persons named John Provaranjan Chowdhury and Binoy Krishna Sikdar, preferred a total of nine petitions of complaint before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dhaka on 7th September 2008, engaging sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, (henceforth cited as the Act) as amended. The complaint petition was impregnated with the allegation that some 9 (nine) cheques issued on various dates by a joint stock company limited, by shares, named Madaripur Spinning Mills Ltd., was bounced by the concerned Bank on different dates. Terms in all the complaint petitions were identical except such differences as may be called mutatis mutandis. 

 27. Both the, complainants implicated" the Managing Director, the Executive Director, a Director and the Chief Accountant of the company in all the complaint petitions. 

 72. The issue was whether a company was liable for the acts of its senior investment managers, done without the company's knowledge. In that case the employees concerned had the company's authority to commit the offences, and the Privy Council advised that the company is liable. 

 82. The acts of the controlling officer of the company are deemed to be those of the company. The same is true of the officer's state of mind. A company not being a natural person has no mind but others' states of mind are attributed to it. In Meridian, supra, Lord Hoffmann called the methods by which acts and states of mind are imputed to the company, rules of attribution. The decision in Kent & Sussex was approved in for Haulage Ltd [1944] KB 551 (CCA). A company was held liable for conspiracy, then a common law offence. A natural person cannot in general be liable vicariously for a common law crime, yet the company was liable. The court adopted the test of identification. The facts and state of mind of the managing director were held to be those of the company. In Moor vs Bresler Ltd [19447 2 All ER 515, false returns were made in tax forms. The Divisional Court held that the acts of the company secretary and branch managers were to be treated as those of the company. In Meridian Lord Hoffmann advised that the question whose act and state of mind was to be attributed to the company was answered 'by applying the usual canons of interpretation, taking into account the language of the rule (if it is a statute) and its content and policy. 

 83. Moore raises the issue of whether the activities of all employees are deemed to be those of the company. Modern law used to stress that only acts of controlling officers were taken to be those of the company. The metaphor often used was 'brain' and 'hands', terms which derive front the civil law judgment of Denning LJ (as he then was), in Bolton (Engineering) Co Ltd vs TJ Graham & Sons Ltd [1957] 1 QB 159. The company was liable only for the forbidden acts or omissions of its 'brain', and not for those of its 'hands.' This point was emphasized in Meridian where Lord Hoffman advised that the policy behind the statute had to be investigated to determine whether a certain person's acts and state of mind were to be attributed to the company. For example, in Moore vs I Bresler Ltd the court was right in attributing the mens rea of the servant authorised to complete the returns to the company, but that ruling did not automatically apply to other crimes such as manslaughter, which in Tesco vs Nattrass, supra, turned on the words of the relevant statute and did not lay down a general rule. In Worthy vs Gordon Plant (Services) Ltd [1989] RTR 7 (DC) the actus reus and mens rea of a traffic manager were imputed to a company. This case demonstrates that the identification doctrine is not limited to directors, as Lord Diplock thought in Tesco vs Nattrass:, nor to employees of the company: the manager was self-employed; nevertheless, the company was liable. Ships's master: re P&O Ferrier (Dover) Ltd (1991) 93 Cr App R 72; European Sales Manager of a company's aircraft division; Redfern [1993] Crim. 

 85. Lord Reid looked for the substance of the transaction, not just at the form as Lord Diplock did. He instanced the board of directions, the managing director and perhaps other superior officers [who] speak and act as the company. Tesco vs Nattrass must now be seen as a case of statutory interpretation: Meridian. The manager was not a 'brain', for the purpose of the relevant statute. A manager may be a 'brain' for another purpose. 

 86. An important application of the identification doctrine took place in P&O European Ferries (Dover) Ltd. supra. The case arose out of the sinking of the Herald of Free Enterprise at Zeebrugge. The assistant bosun, who was asleep when the ship was leaving the harbour, and chief officer, who should have checked whether the bow doors were closed but could not because he was on the bridge, were not senior enough for their alleged carelessness to be deemed to be the carelessness of the company. The failure to prove carelessness against senior management meant that the trial of the company for manslaughter collapsed. Woolf J (as he then was) in Essendon Engineering Co Ltd vs Maile [1982] RTR 260 held it is the judge who decides whether a person is 'brain' or 'hand'. 

 90. In Director of Public Prosecution vs Kent and Sussex Contractor Ltd, 1944 1 KB 146, Viscount Caldecote, the Lord Chief Justice, and Macnaghten and Hal let JJ held that the trial Judge was wrong and that the company could be convicted of the offence created by Motor Fuel Rationing Order 1941. 

 99; Denning LJ in HL Bolton (Engineering) Co. Ltd. vs TJ Graham & Sons Ltd. [1957] 1 QB 159, 172 on Brain and Hand theory; "A company may in' many .ways be likened to a human body. It has a brain and nerve centre which controls what it does. It also has hands which hold the tools and act in accordance with directions from the' centre. Some of the people in the company are mere servants and agents who are nothing more than hands to do the work and cannot be said to represent the mind or will. Others are directors and managers who represent the directing mind and will of the company, and control what it does. The state of mind of these managers is the state of mind of the company and is treated by the law as such." 

 100. When Denning LJ referred to directors and managers representing the directing mind and will of the company, he must have meant, those who constitute the directing mind and will, not all employees. 

 105. It observed,"Before turning to Mr Lissack's (AG's Counsel) submission in relation to personal liability it is convenient first to refer to the speech of Lord Hoffmann in Meridian Global Funds Management Asia Ltd. vs Securities Commission [1995] 2 AC 500, on which Mr Lissack relied as the ,linchpin of this part of his argument. It was a case in which the chief investment officer and senior portfolio manager of an investment management company, with the company's authority but unknown to the board of directors and managing director, used funds managed by the company to acquire shares, but failed to comply with a statutory obligation to give notice of the acquisition to the Securities Commission. The trial judge held that the knowledge of the officer and manager should be attributed to the company, and the Court of Appeal of New Zealand upheld the decision on the basis that the officer was the directing mind and will of the company. The Privy Council dismissed an appeal. Lord Hoffmann, giving the 'judgment of the Privy Council, said, at p. 506, that the company's primary rules of attribution were generally found in its constitution or implied by company law. But, in an exceptional case, where the application of these principles would defeat the intended application of a particular provision to companies, it was necessary to devise rule of attribution". 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (I), where any offence, under this Act has been committed by a company and. it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and pun is hed accordingly." 

 133. Section 20(1) of the same Act, on the other hand, stipulates, "Where an offence under this Act, which has been committed by a body corporate, is proved to have been committed with the consent and connivance of or to the (sic) today neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other similar officer of the body corporate, or any person who was purporting to act in any such capacity, he, as well as the body corporate, or any person who was purporting to act in any such capacity, he as well as the body corporate shall be guilty of that offence and'shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished." 

 140. Sub-section (2) of section ·140 of the Act makes it even more clearly by providing that such "director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be liable who "consents" or "connives" to the commission of the offence committed by the company.
